analysis.one_liner: Bars companies from forcing data breach victims into private arbitration instead of court.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and died when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When companies get hacked and customers' personal data is stolen, the fine print in most customer agreements forces those customers into private arbitration — a confidential process with no judge, no jury, and limited appeal — instead of allowing them to sue in court. This bill would have banned that practice for data breach disputes, voiding existing clauses and giving breach victims the right to sue in court, recover attorney's fees, and enlist the FTC and state attorneys general in enforcement.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers whose sensitive personal data is exposed in a breach — Social Security numbers, bank account numbers, biometric identifiers — who would regain the ability to take companies to court, including as part of a class action, rather than being funneled into individual, confidential arbitration.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits companies from requiring individuals to agree to arbitrate disputes related to a security breach, including identity theft, as a condition of a customer agreement [S2][S3].
Voids existing arbitration clauses covering security breaches, so the ban applies to agreements signed before enactment [S3].
Creates a private right of action letting injured individuals sue for damages, restitution, and injunctive relief, with attorney's fees and expert witness fees recoverable from liable companies [S3].
Adds FTC enforcement treating violations as unfair or deceptive practices, plus state attorney general enforcement on behalf of residents [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that hold consumer data — banks, retailers, credit bureaus, tech platforms — would face courtroom exposure, including class actions and joint liability for individual officers, and would lose the private, low-cost arbitration channel. Arbitration providers would lose breach-related business.

drawbacks.text: Companies could face broad litigation exposure: the bill imposes joint and several liability on individual executives, directors, and employees who materially aid a violation, and covers a wide range of data including usernames and email/password combinations [S3].

Industry's standard counterargument is that court litigation, especially class actions, is slower and costlier and often benefits plaintiffs' lawyers more than the victims, whose individual breach losses can be small; arbitration is defended as a faster, lower-cost path to individual recovery (general policy debate, not in the provided sources).
The bill addresses only data breach disputes, leaving forced arbitration clauses intact for every other kind of consumer dispute with the same company [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — restoring court access for people whose identities and accounts are compromised — is real, since forced arbitration clauses typically block both individual suits and class actions. The costs fall on companies and, indirectly, potentially on consumers through compliance and legal expenses; critics would add that broad executive liability and wide breach definitions could invite litigation that doesn't help victims much. On balance this is a straightforward consumer rights bill whose main trade-off is higher legal exposure for data-holding firms.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its digital commerce subcommittee, and neither ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ted Lieu introduced the bill on March 5, 2018, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1][S5].
Four days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Digital Commerce and Consumer Protection, where it remained without a hearing, markup, or floor vote [S5].
The bill had no cosponsors [S4], and the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, killing the bill under the rule that legislation does not carry over between Congresses [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that collect consumer data keep the ability to route breach victims into private arbitration, and arbitration providers keep that stream of business; no consumer gained anything, because the bill never advanced.

for.name: Rep. Ted Lieu
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Greg Walden (R) in the 115th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never held a hearing or markup on the bill.

against.name: Subcommittee on Digital Commerce and Consumer Protection
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral on March 9, 2018, and took no further action.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no voting record exists; it had a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors from either party, and sat in a Republican-controlled committee.

industries.industry: Companies that collect and hold consumer data (banks, retailers, tech platforms, credit bureaus)
industries.note: The bill would strip their ability to force breach victims out of court, exposing them to damages suits, class actions, and recovery of victims' attorney fees. Keeping forced arbitration in place saves them legal costs at the direct expense of breach victims' court access.

Mandatory arbitration clauses generate a steady pipeline of consumer disputes routed to private arbitrators; banning them for data breach disputes would remove that business. Their interest lies with the companies that draft the clauses, not with consumers forced into the process.
